narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated an 80% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, the admissions decision treated that high estimated risk as a reason not to offer you a place.

The strongest factor driving this prediction was your LSAT score. Your score of 19 is far below the average of about 37 among students who were accepted, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward bar-exam failure. The second most influential factor was your year-three class standing: you are in the first decile, compared with an accepted-student average around the sixth decile. That also pushed toward failure. The third factor was your year-one class standing, again first decile versus an accepted average near the sixth decile, which reinforced the same concern. All three leading factors pointed in the same direction—toward a higher chance of failing the bar—so there was no strong counterbalancing signal in the model’s top considerations. Other personal details, including family income and full-time status, were not among the leading reasons for the denial.

To improve your chances in a future application, focus first on substantially preparing for and retaking the LSAT, since it was the single largest influence. Meet with a pre-law advisor to discuss your academic record and whether an explanatory addendum is appropriate. Consider delaying reapplication until you can present stronger evidence, and ask admissions offices for feedback so your next application directly addresses these concerns.
